name: The Glissando Throat

detectability.signature: Paired starfield images with fixed parallax error; aperture-cycle electromagnetic bursts every 19 hours

proximity: Starfield doubles: one image native, one refracted from the far mouth
Navigational computers log impossible parallax readings near the mouth
contact: Transit drags the ship along a luminous corridor of stretched starlight
Chronometers drift by fractions of seconds during passage
prolonged_exposure: Repeated transits leave crews with persistent double memories
Exit coordinates wander further apart with each successive crossing

age: approximately 340 years since reactivation; builder unknown
phenomena: Doubled starfield showing native and far-side views at once
Impossible parallax readings on navigation instruments
Exotic particle traces and ozone signatures at each aperture opening
known_incidents: First certified human transit in 2314 returned its crew eleven seconds before they departed, on schedule and deeply unsettled.
description: A corridor of stretched starlight hangs between two anchor rings of alien basalt, three hundred forty meters across, its walls flowing like poured glass. Through the mouth a different sky is plainly visible, doubled and slightly delayed. Sensors taste ozone and something like old mathematics.

The throat opens and closes on a nineteen-hour cycle, sliding transit windows across the day like a scale played on organ pipes. A crossing takes eleven subjective seconds, though chronometers emerge drifting by fractions and exit points wander a few thousand kilometers per passage. Navigators describe the ride as being pronounced correctly by something enormous.

The basalt rings predate every neighboring civilization, yet the mechanism still runs, and fragmentary archives at the near mouth describe a builder fleeing something unseen. First certified human transit in 2314 returned its crew eleven seconds before they departed, precisely on schedule and deeply unsettled. The far mouth opens into a cluster otherwise unreachable within a lifetime.

Convoys now queue for each aperture with the discipline of the frightened, while smugglers pay premiums for unscheduled slots. Translation of the archive continues, slowed by argument over whether the builders escaped or failed. Transit logs grow stranger the longer anyone studies them.
